statement: A compression profile is purely a creation-time policy: it is never required by, recorded as required in, or consulted during decompression.
research_needed: Conformance test: archives from all four profiles decode with one reader that has no profile knowledge.

statement: The archive must record every transform, codec, parameter and dictionary needed to reconstruct its content.
research_needed: Corpus test that no reconstruction input is implicit (e.g. codec default levels/windows) across all profiles.

statement: Any decoder implementing an archive's declared features must be able to decode archives from any profile without being told which profile produced them.
research_needed: Cross-profile decode conformance matrix against an independent reader.

statement: The CLI has no --profile flag on unpack and never will; the source calls profile-independence of decoding the most important user-facing property of the compression system.
A profile is exactly an assignment to a fixed set of named parameters (the constrained objective of §5.4); the parameter set is fixed in this section, only the values are deferred.
refines_or_supersedes: Refines §5.4 (profile as constrained objective) into a named parameter set

statement: Numeric values for every profile parameter (decode rate, memory, window, access granularity, lookback, budget, chunk sizes, etc.) are deferred to §25.3.
research_needed: Benchmark corpus measurement of ratio/decode-rate/memory trade-offs per profile on declared reference hardware.
decision_needed: What concrete values does each of fast/balanced/dense/extreme assign to each of the thirteen parameters?

statement: Parameter min_decode_rate: floor on decompression throughput, measured in logical bytes per second per core on a declared reference machine.
research_needed: Define and publish reference machine; measure codec/transform decode rates on it.

statement: The declared reference machine for min_decode_rate is not defined, nor how a planner guarantees a throughput floor deterministically without timing (budget is not seconds).
research_needed: Model-based decode-rate prediction per codec/level validated against measurements on several CPUs.
decision_needed: Which reference machine is declared, and is min_decode_rate enforced by a static codec cost model rather than timing?

statement: Parameter max_decode_memory: byte ceiling on decoder working set; it becomes the archive's declared DecodeRequirements.
research_needed: Measure actual decoder peak memory for each codec/window/transform combination vs declared value.

statement: Parameter max_decode_window: byte ceiling on any codec window; the window must be recorded and never left to a codec default.
Parameter max_access_granularity: worst-case bytes decoded to read one arbitrary byte; it drives the access_cost declaration of §7.5.
Parameter max_lookback, in chunks, bounds chunk-group dependency depth.
compress_budget is expressed in candidate evaluations and bytes examined, explicitly not in seconds (per §5.7).
research_needed: Show that budget-in-work-units yields identical output across machines and thread counts.

statement: Parameters chunk_size_target, min and max (bytes, per content category) are the CDC parameters a profile sets.
Parameter dictionary_policy takes one of none, supplied, or train-if-measured-to-pay.
research_needed: Define the deterministic measurement rule for when a trained dictionary 'pays' (including dictionary storage cost).

statement: Parameter transform_classes is a subset of {structural, reconstructive}, governing which transforms may be applied.
Parameter codec_candidates is a subset of the registered codec set and defines the planner search space.
Parameter evaluation_mode is sampled or full: whether codec candidates are measured on samples or on real data.
Parameter clustering_mode (none / cheap-ordering / full-similarity) controls chunk ordering; it is a profile parameter because ordering is format-visible via grouping (§5.2).
Parameter chunking_strategy_search (single / multiple) controls whether several chunking assignments are evaluated end-to-end; needed because extreme evaluates more than one chunking.
Every profile assigns all thirteen parameters.
The archive records the resulting DecodeRequirements and access_cost, not the profile name, so decoders never need to know which profile made an archive.

Ambiguities: 'thirteen' counts chunk_size_target/min/max (per category) as one parameter; §6.0 forbids recording the profile 'as required' but §6.0a says the profile is not recorded at all, leaving informational recording undecided.
decision_needed: May an archive record the creating profile name informationally (e.g. in the conversion record), and how are per-category chunk parameters structured?

statement: Sampled evaluation and 'where measured to pay' decisions must remain deterministic; the sampling rule and pay-off test are not specified here.
research_needed: Specify deterministic sample selection and pay-off thresholds; test reproducibility across thread counts and platforms.
decision_needed: What deterministic sampling and pay-off rules does the planner use?

statement: Chunk padding policy (--pad) and boundary mode (--chunk-boundary) change stored size and chunking but are not among the thirteen profile parameters; their relation to profiles is unstated.
decision_needed: Are padding policy and chunk-boundary mode profile-independent options, profile parameters, or planner objective inputs?

statement: fast profile: throughput and low resource use dominate; single-pass analysis with only a cheap incompressibility probe and no deep categorisation.
fast profile uses content-defined chunking with one parameter set for all content, no per-category tuning.
refines_or_supersedes: Narrows §7.2/§7.3 per-category CDC: fast deliberately uses a single parameter set

statement: fast profile performs exact chunk dedup only and no clustering: input order is preserved.
fast profile trains no dictionaries but uses a pre-supplied dictionary if given.
fast profile applies structural transforms only, and only where detection is free.
fast profile does no codec search: one high-throughput codec at a low level; the codec is not named.
decision_needed: Which codec and level is fast's single codec?

statement: fast profile uses lookback 0: every chunk independently decodable.
fast profile targets very high decode throughput with small, fixed decode memory and the finest random-access granularity of any profile.
research_needed: Measure fast's decode throughput/memory vs zstd-low and LZ4 baselines.

statement: fast is suited to CI build artifacts, intermediate pipeline data, and archives written and read within minutes.
research_needed: Benchmark fast against tar+zstd/LZ4 in CI workloads.

statement: balanced is the default profile for entrybound pack and the profile against which the others are justified; intended for any use.
balanced profile performs full content categorisation and uses per-category CDC parameters.
balanced profile uses exact chunk dedup plus cheap similarity ordering within directories and categories.
balanced trains dictionaries for cohorts of many small similar files, only where measured to pay.
research_needed: Measure dictionary gain thresholds by cohort size and file size.
decision_needed: What cohort size / expected gain threshold triggers dictionary training?

statement: balanced fully enables structural transforms; reconstructive transforms are enabled where detection is cheap and verification passes.
balanced uses a small codec candidate set with sampled evaluation.
balanced uses lookback 0 by default; a small bounded lookback is available via --lookback=N but not default, to preserve §13.2's parallel-decode and random-access guarantees.
refines_or_supersedes: Tied to §13.2 claims for default configuration

statement: The bound on --lookback=N ('small bounded') is unspecified, as is whether it overrides max_lookback on other profiles and how it reports the resulting access_cost.
decision_needed: What is the maximum N for --lookback on balanced, and is the flag valid for all profiles?

statement: balanced targets fast decode with a modest declared memory ceiling; random access is preserved and granularity declared.
dense profile (substantially smaller, still practical to read) performs full categorisation plus cross-file similarity analysis.
dense tunes chunking per category, using smaller chunks where dedup pays.
research_needed: Measure dedup gain vs index cost (§7.3) per category to define 'pays'.

statement: dense uses exact chunk dedup plus similarity-directed grouping, and full similarity clustering across the whole archive.
Full archive-wide similarity clustering (dense/extreme) has unstated time/memory complexity and determinism guarantees for archives larger than RAM.
research_needed: Evaluate MinHash/LSH-style clustering for bounded memory and deterministic output on multi-TB corpora.
decision_needed: What clustering algorithm and memory bound do dense/extreme use?

statement: dense trains dictionaries per cohort, allowing multiple dictionaries per archive.
dense applies all structural and reconstructive transforms, with verification mandatory.
dense performs wide codec candidate and parameter search on real data, not samples.
dense uses a larger declared lookback; the access-granularity cost is computed and recorded.
decision_needed: What lookback value does dense declare?

statement: dense declares higher but still bounded decode memory; random access preserved but coarser, with granularity declared in the descriptor.
dense suits software distribution, release artifacts, container images, and write-once read-many use.
research_needed: Compare dense against xz/zstd-19 tarballs and OCI layer compression on release corpora.

statement: extreme profile (minimum size, compression time nearly free) performs exhaustive analysis, evaluating multiple chunking strategies end-to-end.
extreme trains multiple candidate dictionaries and selects by measured outcome.
extreme applies all transforms including expensive reconstructive ones, all verified.
extreme performs full codec search over the registered set, including archival-tier codecs.
extreme searches 'archival-tier codecs', yet the best archival-tier compressors are said to fail §5.8; which archival-tier codecs actually pass the registry criteria is unstated.
research_needed: Evaluate candidate high-ratio codecs (e.g. context-mixing, LZMA-class) against §5.8 criteria: spec, portability, memory, licence.
decision_needed: Which archival-tier codecs, if any, enter the registered set for extreme?

statement: extreme permits large groups; access granularity is the coarsest, computed, declared, and reported/printed to the user at pack time.
extreme's compression budget is 'effectively unbounded', but compress_budget is a counted work budget; the finite value, termination, and reproducibility for extreme are unspecified.
decision_needed: What finite compress_budget does extreme assign, and is extreme output reproducible across machines?

statement: extreme's dimension table omits Chunking, Dedup, Clustering and Decode-target rows, so its clustering_mode, chunk sizes and dedup behaviour are unspecified despite 'every profile assigns all thirteen'.
decision_needed: What are extreme's chunking, dedup and clustering assignments?

statement: extreme's decode requirements are still declared, bounded and validated; it trades compression time and random-access granularity for size, never decodability.
The concrete decode-memory bound for extreme and what 'validated' means (writer self-check, reader refusal against a local budget, or both) are not specified here.
decision_needed: What is the maximum declared decode memory for any Entrybound archive, and who validates it?

statement: extreme is bounded by the §5.8 registry criteria; compressors those criteria exclude are not shipped by Entrybound.
The archival-tier compressors reaching best ratios have 8-31 GiB decode footprints, non-portable floating-point-dependent behaviour, or licences incompatible with redistribution.
research_needed: Cite primary benchmarks/licences for top-ratio compressors (e.g. Large Text Compression Benchmark leaders).

statement: extreme suits long-term archival, cold storage, and very-large-scale distribution where bytes multiply across millions of downloads.
research_needed: Quantify extreme's gain over dense and incumbents; assess decoder longevity for archival use.

statement: Extracting a Complete Entrybound archive reproduces every original file byte-for-byte; no mode, profile, flag or extension is exempt.
research_needed: End-to-end round-trip fuzzing across profiles, transforms and codecs.

statement: Archive role is declared in the preamble (§4.2 item 9), participates in identity, and must be determinable by a reader from the preamble before any other processing.
A Sidecar makes no extraction claim; unpack refuses a Sidecar and explains why.
An Incremental archive references a base archive and requires it for extraction.
Complete is the default role and what entrybound pack produces; only Complete archives carry the byte-exactness guarantee.
Only Complete archives carry the byte-exact guarantee; whether extracting an Incremental archive with its base present carries the same guarantee is unstated.
decision_needed: Does the losslessness contract extend to Incremental archives when all bases are available and verified?

statement: For File entries the extracted octets equal the octets read at creation; for Symlink the target octets are identical; verified end-to-end by logical_digest independent of transforms and codecs.

The formal contract covers only File and Symlink; handling of other EntryKinds, and of targets that cannot represent a path or symlink (refused or confined extraction), versus 'no mode in which this is not true', is unresolved.
research_needed: Platform matrix of extraction outcomes where a path or symlink cannot be materialised.
decision_needed: Is a refused or renamed extraction a contract violation, a declared fidelity gap, or out of scope?

statement: Metadata fidelity is a separate axis (§10) and is explicitly not guaranteed complete, since no target platform can restore every source platform's metadata.
Every metadata fidelity gap must be declared (I13).
Semantic-only (payload-lossless, file-lossy) transformations do not exist in Entrybound, not even with explicit opt-in; re-encoding content is the user's job before archiving.
Mainstream tools that 'losslessly recompress' PNGs and gzip streams are lossless about payload but lossy about the file, and users routinely do not know the difference.
research_needed: Survey tools (e.g. PNG optimisers, gzip recompressors) and user-understanding evidence.

statement: Reconstructive transforms already deliver roughly a fifth off JPEG and meaningful gains on deflate-containing formats, bit-exactly.
research_needed: Measure bit-exact JPEG recompression (Lepton/brunsli-class) and deflate reconstruction (preflate-class) on a representative corpus.

statement: The extra gain from true lossy re-encoding is small relative to the loss of a clean losslessness contract.
research_needed: Quantify lossy re-encode gains vs bit-exact reconstructive gains per format.

statement: An Entrybound archive of JPEGs will not be smaller than a specialist lossy re-encoder's output, and §23 makes no such claim.
Entrybound must not simply repeat the solid-archive trade (single-file reads decode all predecessors, damage destroys everything after) nor dismiss the ratio solid grouping buys.
The most-used solid format's vendor documentation states single-file extraction analyses all preceding files and a damaged region destroys everything after it.
evidence_in_source: secondary reference to vendor documentation (not cited inline)
research_needed: Cite the vendor documentation section precisely.

statement: Content-addressed chunks are native and structural; every other dedup mechanism depends on them.
Exact chunk deduplication is native and always on; in STREAM layout its reach is bounded by stream_dedup_window (§4.6).
The value and semantics of stream_dedup_window, and how the bounded reach in STREAM layout squares with 'always on' exact dedup claims per profile, are not set here.
research_needed: Measure dedup loss vs window size on streamed inputs.
decision_needed: What stream_dedup_window default and maximum apply?

statement: Content-defined chunking is native with per-category parameters, chosen for insertion resilience over fixed blocks.
Shared dictionaries are native, first-class archive objects.
Shared dictionaries are the only way small-file cohorts compress well without solid grouping.
research_needed: Compare dictionaries vs small lookback groups vs similarity ordering on small-file corpora.

statement: Independently decodable chunks are the native default, for random access, parallel decode and corruption containment.
Chunk groups with declared lookback are native: the solid trade made explicit and bounded as a dial.
Similarity clustering is planner behaviour adding no format structure, though ordering determines grouping and therefore stored size and access granularity (§5.2).
Cross-archive and cross-tenant deduplication is rejected (rationale in §9.7).
Fixed-size blocking is rejected in favour of content-defined chunking.
A widely-deployed packaging format uses fixed 64 KB blocks for differential update and its vendor guidance tells developers to confine changes within block boundaries.
evidence_in_source: quoted vendor guidance (source not cited inline)
research_needed: Cite the packaging-format vendor guidance document.

statement: Chunking parameters are per content category, selected by the planner, and recorded in the archive.
Deployed systems: backup tools shipping a chunk index to clients choose MiB-scale averages; HTTP content-distribution systems 64 KiB-1 MiB; research benchmarks 2-16 KiB.
evidence_in_source: survey of deployed systems (not individually cited)
research_needed: Cite each system and parameter; confirm current defaults.

statement: For one published 37 GB dataset: 64 KiB average gave ~378k chunks and 20 MB index; 1 MiB ~26k chunks, 1.3 MB; 8 MiB ~4.3k chunks, 327 KB; stored size barely moved.
research_needed: Reproduce on Entrybound's corpus with its chunk-table entry size.

statement: Past the point where dedup stops paying, smaller chunks buy nothing and cost index size.
research_needed: Measure dedup-vs-index curves across content categories and archive sizes.

statement: The planner must model index (chunk table) size as part of stored size.
Normalised chunking is used to control chunk-size variance.
Published measurements put the normalised-chunking sweet spot at roughly 60% variance reduction for under 2% dedup loss; the normalisation level chosen is not stated.
research_needed: Cite source (FastCDC-class paper); measure normalisation levels on Entrybound corpus.
decision_needed: Which normalisation level does the v1 chunker use?

statement: Chunker variants with boundary-skipping optimisations that accept a chunk on a partial feature match are excluded regardless of throughput, as silent-corruption risks.
The chunker is not upgradable in place: Entrybound versions and declares the chunker from v1, and a chunker change is a feature-flagged format evolution.
A major backup project declined to fix a real chunker weakness because changing the chunker breaks dedup against existing data.
research_needed: Cite the project issue/response.

statement: The v1 CDC algorithm, rolling hash, normalisation level, and default per-category size ranges are not selected in this section.
research_needed: Benchmark candidate CDC algorithms (Gear/FastCDC-class, etc.) for throughput, dedup and boundary-security under keyed variants.
decision_needed: Which chunking algorithm and parameter defaults are frozen as chunker v1?

statement: The content-category taxonomy that per-category CDC parameters key on is undefined, including whether categorisation is deterministic and recorded.
decision_needed: What content categories exist and is category assignment recorded in the archive?

statement: extreme evaluates multiple chunking strategies and parameters are per category, yet PCR binds 'the chunking parameters' and the chunker is declared once; whether one archive may mix chunker versions/parameter sets and how PCR binds them is unclear.
decision_needed: Can a single archive contain multiple chunker algorithms/parameter sets, and how are they encoded in the PCR descriptor?

statement: The chunk table is the dedup index and lives in the archive; its size is a first-class planner input.
For very large archives the chunk table is itself chunked and compressed.
The chunk table need not be resident to decode: offset-to-chunk resolution needs only entries for the range being read; the index is range-addressable from the start.
research_needed: Verify decode memory independent of archive size on multi-TB archives.

statement: A flat in-RAM chunk index is the most persistent mistake in dedup backup tools; the leading tool spent multiple release cycles on faster index loading and lower memory.
evidence_in_source: historical reference (tool not named, no citation)
research_needed: Cite release notes of the referenced backup tool.

statement: The 'very large' threshold for chunking the chunk table and its range-addressable structure (paging, sort key, lookup path) are unspecified.
decision_needed: What on-disk structure and threshold does the chunked chunk table use?

statement: Writer-side memory for always-on exact dedup is unaddressed: the reader need not hold the index, but pack must look up every chunk digest seen so far.
research_needed: Measure pack memory for exact dedup over billions of chunks; evaluate external/sharded dedup tables with deterministic output.
decision_needed: What is the pack-time memory bound for exact dedup, and what happens when it is exceeded?

statement: A ChunkGroup comprises group_id, max_lookback (count of preceding chunks whose state a member may depend on) and access_cost (an AccessCostDeclaration).
ChunkGroup membership is declared by Chunk.group_ref and nowhere else (§3.5).
max_lookback = 0 (every chunk independently decodable) is the default for fast and balanced, which is why §13.2's parallel-decode and random-access claims hold by default.
With max_lookback = k, reading a chunk may require decoding up to k preceding chunks in the same group; used by dense and extreme.
The codec-level mechanism for lookback k is undefined: what 'state' means, how dependency stays within k rather than chaining transitively, and interaction with codec windows and parallel decode.
research_needed: Prototype lookback via prefix-dictionary/reference framing in zstd-class codecs; measure ratio vs k.
decision_needed: How is bounded lookback realised in the codec framing so that the declared bound is enforceable by readers?

statement: access_cost must state in the archive the worst-case number of chunks and bytes decoded to read one arbitrary chunk.
entrybound inspect prints access_cost.
entrybound pack prints access_cost at the end of a dense or extreme run.

Where and in what unit access cost lives is inconsistent: per-ChunkGroup access_cost (chunks+bytes per chunk), archive-recorded access_cost, 'granularity declared in the descriptor', and max_access_granularity in bytes per byte.
decision_needed: Is access cost declared per group, per archive in the descriptor, or both, and with which unit?

statement: Corruption containment follows group boundaries: a damaged chunk destroys only its group's dependent chunks, and entrybound verify reports exactly which entries are affected.
§7.5 says a damaged chunk destroys 'its group's dependent chunks'; §8.7 narrows this to at most k following dependent chunks, not the whole group. The precise blast radius needs one definition.
decision_needed: Is corruption blast radius defined as k following chunks or all dependents within the group?

statement: Invariant I24: in an encrypted archive, physical chunk boundaries must not leak plaintext structure.

Two 2025 results broke seed-randomised CDC: secret chunking parameters of three deployed backup tools were recovered from encrypted chunk sizes, enabling file fingerprinting and extraction of low-entropy content.
evidence_in_source: primary research results (papers not cited inline)
research_needed: Cite both 2025 papers and confirm attack models apply to Entrybound's threat model.

statement: One paper concluded seed-based boundary randomisation is not generically secure; remedies: pad chunks to maximum/bucketed size, or encrypt the rolling hash before boundary comparison at 50-160% chunking overhead.
research_needed: Cite paper; reproduce overhead measurement with hardware AES.

statement: Vendor responses to the 2025 attacks: one fixed the chunker the same day, one mitigated within weeks, one declined because changing the chunker breaks dedup against existing repositories.
research_needed: Cite vendor advisories.

statement: Unencrypted archives use CDC with unpadded chunk sizes, since sizes leak nothing the plaintext does not already reveal.
Encrypted archives by default pad chunk sizes to declared buckets; storage cost is bounded and declared; the size sequence is quantised, not hidden, and residual leakage is real and unquantified.
The bucket schedule (bucket boundaries) and the declared storage-cost bound for default padding are not specified; effectiveness is routed to security review.
research_needed: Quantify fingerprinting resistance vs overhead for candidate bucket schedules (e.g. power-of-two, Padme-class).
decision_needed: Which bucket schedule is the default and what overhead bound is declared?

statement: Encrypted archives support --pad=max: all chunks padded to the maximum size (highest cost, strongest hiding).
--pad=none is an explicit opt-out; the archive records that sizes are unpadded, and inspect and verify report it as a declared leak.
Encrypted-archive chunk boundaries are derived under a key-domain secret as defence in depth; padding, not the secret, is the relied-upon mechanism.
The difference between default boundary derivation under a key-domain secret and the --chunk-boundary=keyed-prf mode is not specified; both are keyed.
decision_needed: What exactly does each mode compute (seeded gear table vs PRF over rolling-hash output), and which key-derivation label feeds each?

statement: Per the literature, pad-to-maximum mitigates without formal guarantee; Entrybound's default bucketed padding is weaker still, since a bucket sequence is a lower-resolution size sequence.
research_needed: Formal/empirical leakage quantification of bucketed padding against chunk-size fingerprinting.

statement: The published fingerprinting attack needed only two chunk sizes to identify a file.
research_needed: Test whether bucketed size sequences of realistic lengths still identify files.

statement: The default padding approach was chosen on cost, knowingly weaker than the provably-secure keyed rolling-hash construction.
I24 is a design objective, not a delivered proof; §9.8 records chunk-size leakage as quantised rather than hidden.
research_needed: External security review of encrypted CDC leakage.

statement: --chunk-boundary=keyed-prf provides the provably-secure boundary construction; off by default due to cost; recommended when the threat model includes the storage provider.
decision_needed: Should keyed-prf become default for any mode or profile given measured cost?

statement: keyed-prf is described as provably secure at 50-160% chunking overhead partly absorbed by hardware acceleration; whether Entrybound's construction matches the paper's proof assumptions and cost is unverified.
research_needed: Security proof review mapping keyed-prf to the paper; benchmark overhead on AES-NI/ARMv8 and non-accelerated CPUs.

statement: The padding schedule's measured effectiveness is routed to security review (§25.2); this section does not pre-announce its conclusion.
research_needed: External cryptographic review with empirical fingerprinting experiments.
decision_needed: Does the security review accept bucketed padding as the encrypted default?

statement: Physical padding only helps if chunk-table fields are hidden: plaintext chunk digests, logical_len, and duplicate-reference structure in the chunk table would leak sizes and equality unless encrypted; not addressed here.
research_needed: Leakage analysis of every cleartext field in encrypted archives, including hole chunks and within-archive dedup references.
decision_needed: Which chunk-table fields are encrypted, and are plaintext chunk digests ever exposed in encrypted archives?

statement: The §8.0 integrity/identity table is normative and authoritative; every claim elsewhere about what survives what resolves against it and it supersedes looser statements.
refines_or_supersedes: Supersedes any looser statement elsewhere in the specification

statement: Chunk digest is over plaintext chunk bytes; it does not participate in LAI, participates in PCI, and is signature-covered via chunk_root.
ContentObject logical_digest is over the plaintext byte sequence, independent of chunking; it participates in LAI and is signed via LAI.
ContentObject chunk_root is a Merkle root over the ordered chunk list; it does not participate in LAI and is signed as a separate field (via PCR).
Entry identity_digest covers path, kind, logical_digest, ContentRef kind and the metadata the active identity profile includes; it participates in LAI.
Entry aux_digest covers every metadata item the identity profile excludes (timestamps, ownership, modes, ACLs, xattrs, platform metadata); not in LAI; signed via AUX.
Manifest root is a Merkle root over entries in canonical order (§3.4) and participates in LAI.
LAI is a digest over a descriptor binding manifest root, identity-profile ID, archive role, entry count and total logical size; it is signed.
PCR (physical content root) is a descriptor binding every ContentObject chunk_root, chunk count and chunking parameters; not in LAI; signed as a separate field.
AUX is a descriptor binding the Merkle root over all entry aux_digests, the fidelity-report digest and the conversion-record digest; not in LAI; signed.
PCI is the digest of the serialised container bytes; it is signature-covered only if the file itself is signed.
Three signed roots: LAI (same content under this identity profile?), PCR (same chunking of that content?), AUX (same non-identity metadata, fidelity and provenance?).
PCR is a root over the plaintext chunk list, not over container bytes: recompressing without re-chunking leaves it unchanged; the physical file hash is PCI.
Every byte of every entry's metadata is under exactly one of LAI or AUX, so nothing an archive asserts is unsigned (prevents rewriting modes/ACLs/timestamps or stripping fidelity reports).
Contradiction: posix.sparse_hint is metadata said to participate in no digest and no identity, violating 'every byte of metadata is under exactly one of LAI or AUX'.
decision_needed: Is posix.sparse_hint covered by aux_digest (signed) or explicitly exempted with the invariant amended?

statement: §8.0 says AUX is a separate signature binding and verifiers report which root changed, but §8.1 (and §9.6 L1117, L1486) place AUX inside the content binding with LAI, so an AUX change and an LAI change both show as C stale.
refines_or_supersedes: Conflicts with §9.6 L1117/L1486 (content_binding over LAI and AUX)
decision_needed: Does the content binding sign LAI and AUX as separately verifiable fields so verify can say which changed?

statement: The three-way root split corrects an earlier draft whose single content digest claimed two mutually exclusive properties: identity surviving re-chunking and partial reads verifiable against a signed root.
refines_or_supersedes: Supersedes earlier draft single content digest

statement: Descriptor field lists for LAI, PCR and AUX omit the digest-algorithm identifier §8.8 requires, and their canonical byte encoding and domain-separation labels are not given here.
decision_needed: What are the exact descriptor fields, order, encoding and domain labels for LAI, PCR and AUX?

statement: A signature carries three bindings from §9.6: C = content, P = physical, A = addressing, each reported separately.
Editorial defect: §8.1 contains an orphaned first table header (LAI/PCR/AUX/PCI/Signature) before the legend sentence, followed by a second header; the table needs repair.
decision_needed: Fix the malformed duplicate table header in §8.1.

statement: Recompress with same chunking: LAI, PCR, AUX unchanged; PCI changes; all three signature bindings remain valid.
repack --layout: LAI, PCR, AUX unchanged; PCI changes; all bindings valid.
repack --rebuild-index: LAI, PCR, AUX unchanged; PCI changes; all bindings valid.
repack --profile re-plans and therefore re-chunks in general: LAI and AUX unchanged, PCR and PCI change, physical binding becomes stale.
Explicit re-chunking: LAI and AUX unchanged, PCR and PCI change, physical binding stale.
repack --strip-provenance: LAI and PCR unchanged; AUX and PCI change; content binding stale.
Re-encrypt / key add / key remove: LAI and AUX unchanged; PCR changes on encrypted archives because boundaries are key-derived; PCI changes; physical and addressing bindings stale, content valid.

If key add/remove changes PCR because a new file key re-derives boundaries, recipient mutation implies full re-chunk and re-encrypt of the payload; whether recipient changes must rotate the file key is unresolved.
research_needed: Measure cost of recipient mutation with and without file-key rotation; security analysis of key-wrap-only recipient changes.
decision_needed: Do key add/remove rotate the file key (re-chunking everything) or only rewrap it (leaving PCR unchanged)?

statement: Non-identity metadata change: LAI and PCR unchanged; AUX and PCI change; content binding stale.
repack --add: LAI, PCR and PCI change, AUX listed as unchanged; content and physical bindings stale, addressing valid.
Content change: LAI, PCR and PCI change, AUX listed unchanged; content and physical bindings stale, addressing valid.
repack --add lists AUX as unchanged, but AUX binds a Merkle root over all entry aux_digests, so adding entries must change it; content changes may also alter the fidelity report.
decision_needed: Correct the §8.1 AUX column for repack --add (and confirm content-change row).

statement: The survival matrix omits operations: identity-affecting metadata change (core.executable, strict-v1 fields), identity-profile change, role change, --lookback or --pad or --chunk-boundary change, and adding a signature.
decision_needed: What are LAI/PCR/AUX/PCI and binding outcomes for these operations?

statement: Because profiles set chunk_size_target, §17.5's --verify-identity checks LAI only, does not and cannot assert PCR continuity, and must say so.

A stale binding is not invalid: verify reports STALE, never VALID and never as whole-signature failure, so consumers can accept re-optimised content while declining verified range reads against an unseen root.

Fidelity report and conversion record must be signed; stripping provenance therefore invalidates the signature, and repack --strip-provenance warns and refuses without --drop-signatures. Corrects an earlier draft.
refines_or_supersedes: Supersedes earlier draft claim that --strip-provenance changed nothing

statement: L914 says strip-provenance 'invalidates' signatures while L912 insists stale is not invalid; and --drop-signatures discards signatures whose physical and addressing bindings remain valid.
decision_needed: Should strip-provenance keep signatures as STALE, drop them, or offer re-signing?

statement: ZIP, 7z and RAR hash only physical bytes, making recompression a breaking change and migration a re-signing event; note ZIP/7z CRC-32s are computed over uncompressed data, so the claim needs qualification.
evidence_in_source: none cited; auditor notes CRC-32 is over uncompressed data in ZIP/7z
research_needed: Examine ZIP/JAR/APK signing, 7z and RAR5 hash scopes precisely.

statement: Content-addressed stores, container image layers, distributed VCS object stores and immutable-OS content stores separated logical from physical identity and so can change encoding without changing identity.
research_needed: Cite OCI, git, OSTree/Nix precedent.

statement: The container-image specification must explicitly warn implementers not to confuse its two digests (compressed blob vs uncompressed content).
research_needed: Cite the OCI image-spec passage.

statement: Entrybound names its identity roots distinctly, prints all of them in inspect, and never displays one where another is meant.
research_needed: Usability review of inspect output for root confusion.

statement: LAI is computed over a declared model subset named by a versioned identity profile recorded in the descriptor.
Whether a metadata item participates in identity depends only on its registered name and the active profile, never on per-item writer choice; registry §20.3 records the including profiles per name.
Metadata names in the open x- namespaces can never participate in any identity profile.

identity/v1 (default) includes the entry set, LogicalPath component bytes and declared encodings, EntryKind, ContentRef kind, logical_digest, symlink target bytes, archive role, and only core.executable as metadata.
identity/v1 excludes all timestamps, ownership, permission bits beyond executable, ACLs, xattrs, hardlink grouping, fidelity report, conversion record, sparse map, and every physical fact.
identity/strict-v1 additionally includes full mode bits, ownership names, mtime and posix.hardlink_group, so a hardlinked tree differs from a tree of identical copies.
The identity profile ID is bound into the LAI descriptor so a verifier knows which question an LAI answers.

core.executable determinism across sources is unaddressed: Windows filesystems and ZIP/7z imports lack a reliable executable bit, so writers on different platforms could compute different identity/v1 LAIs for the same tree.
research_needed: Cross-platform pack experiment: same tree packed on Linux, macOS, Windows and from legacy imports; compare LAI.
decision_needed: How is core.executable derived when the source has no executable bit?

statement: strict-v1 details unspecified: mtime precision and normalisation, ownership names versus numeric ids or SIDs, 'full mode bits' on non-POSIX sources, and whether strict-v1 ships in v1.
decision_needed: What precise canonical forms does strict-v1 use, and is it a v1 deliverable?

statement: Declared path encodings participate in identity/v1, so byte-identical trees with different declared encodings (e.g. from legacy import heuristics) get different LAIs; intent and interplay with import are unstated.
decision_needed: Should declared encodings participate in identity/v1, and how do legacy adapters declare them deterministically?

statement: Editorial inconsistency: identity/v1 exclusions list 'the sparse map', but §8.4 states there is no sparse map (holes are chunks, geometry is posix.sparse_hint).
decision_needed: Replace 'sparse map' with posix.sparse_hint in the identity/v1 exclusion list.

statement: identity/v1's inclusion of kind-specific payloads (e.g. device numbers for special files, directory entries, hardlink targets) is not stated beyond 'entry set' and EntryKind.
decision_needed: Which kind-specific fields of non-File entries participate in identity/v1?

statement: §8.4 says the Entry digest is over 'the entry's canonical serialised form', whereas §8.0 defines two entry digests (identity_digest, aux_digest) over disjoint subsets; the hierarchy row is ambiguous.
decision_needed: Clarify §8.4 Entry row to name identity_digest and aux_digest.

statement: Invariant I22: none of LAI, PCR or AUX is a bare Merkle root; each is a digest over a small descriptor binding a root to the parameters that give it meaning.

Design precedent: the kernel file-integrity subsystem's file digest hashes a descriptor (version, algorithm, block size, salt size, file size, root hash, salt) to avoid ambiguity across files and padding scenarios.
evidence_in_source: primary design precedent (fs-verity; not cited inline)
research_needed: Cite fs-verity documentation.

statement: There is no sparse map: holes are chunks and participate in logical_digest and chunk_root like content, since the zero bytes they produce are content.
Source filesystem hole geometry is carried as the posix.sparse_hint metadata item, which participates in no digest and no identity.

Per-ContentObject chunk_root and the manifest root are bare Merkle roots (only LAI/PCR/AUX get descriptors); verifying ranges against one chunk_root needs a bound chunk count/length, whose source is unstated.
research_needed: Formal check of range-proof soundness against truncated/extended chunk lists per ContentObject.
decision_needed: Is each chunk_root bound with its chunk count and logical length, and where does a range reader obtain them authenticated?

statement: ArchiveRole is one of Complete (all content internal, standalone extractable), Sidecar (External refs describing another artifact), or Incremental (mix; references a base archive).
Archive role is declared in the preamble and participates in LAI, closing the attack where stripping all chunks from a signed Complete archive yields a Sidecar with the same LAI and valid signature.
A Sidecar carries describes_lai (LAI of the described artifact) as a stated claim in its conversion record; its own LAI is over its external-referencing entries and is distinct, never conflated.
Incremental archives are underspecified here: how the base is referenced (LAI, PCR or PCI), chain depth limits, and how base binding is verified.
decision_needed: By which root is an Incremental's base identified, and what verification is required before extraction?

statement: describes_lai lives in the conversion record (covered by AUX, not LAI); how a verifier validates it against the described artifact, and what a Sidecar signature vouches for, is unstated.
decision_needed: What does verifying a Sidecar against its described artifact check, and what does its signature assert?

statement: Merkle trees are built over each ContentObject's ordered chunk list and over the manifest's ordered entry list, with construction rules fixed in the spec.
Merkle leaf and interior nodes are domain-separated with distinct prefixes, preventing leaf/interior collision and subtree-as-leaf presentation (as in certificate transparency).
evidence_in_source: primary precedent (CT tree specification, not cited inline)
decision_needed: What exact prefix bytes are used?

statement: No power-of-two padding: the tree splits at the largest power of two smaller than n, giving a canonical shape and eliminating the duplicate-last-node bug class.
evidence_in_source: precedent: a real consensus vulnerability in a widely-deployed system (not cited inline)
research_needed: Test vectors for n=1..N including n=1 and n=0 handling.
decision_needed: How are empty (n=0) chunk lists and manifests rooted?

statement: Length is bound into the root via the descriptor so a truncated tree is not valid; the text cites §8.3 though the descriptor rule is in §8.4.
refines_or_supersedes: Cross-reference to §8.3 appears to mean §8.4 (I22 descriptor)

statement: Every multi-field hash input is length-prefixed and unambiguously encoded so distinct field decompositions cannot yield the same preimage.
Outboard encoding: the Merkle tree is stored in its own MERKLE_OUTBOARD section separate from payload, so adding verification metadata never rewrites payload and signatures survive an index rebuild.
Range verification: a reader wanting bytes [a,b) fetches the covering chunks plus O(log n) interior nodes on their paths and verifies against the root.
The Merkle outboard costs a small, fixed fraction of archive size; in practice it scales with chunk count, so the fraction varies with chunk size.
research_needed: Measure MERKLE_OUTBOARD size as fraction of archive across profiles and chunk sizes.

statement: Every container-image format chose a flat per-chunk digest list, which requires trusting or fully validating the whole index before random verification.
research_needed: Survey eStargz/zstd:chunked/SOCI/Nydus verification designs.

statement: Both flat per-chunk digests (in the chunk table, for cheap sequential verification) and the Merkle tree (for cheap random verification) are present, consistent by construction since the tree is built over the same digests.

'Consistent by construction' holds only for honest writers; in a crafted archive flat chunk-table digests and MERKLE_OUTBOARD can disagree, and which is authoritative or whether readers must cross-check is unstated.
research_needed: Conformance corpus cases with inconsistent flat digests vs tree; check reader outcomes match.
decision_needed: Which structure is authoritative and what must a conforming reader do on disagreement?

statement: §8.8 prefers a tree-capable hash so 'tree structure and hash agree', but §8.6 fixes a CT-style binary tree over variable-size CDC chunks; how a tree-native hash's internal leaves would agree with CDC chunk leaves is unresolved.
research_needed: Compare SHA-256 + external Merkle vs BLAKE3-class tree hashing for CDC chunk trees (speed, proof size, standardisation).
decision_needed: Is the Merkle tree layered over a conventional hash, or does the chosen tree hash define it?

statement: verify on a damaged archive reports failing chunks, their ContentObjects, referencing Entries, entries affected via group dependency (at most k following chunks), and which entries are intact.
Corruption localisation works without reading the whole archive when an index is present.
Localisation is said to work on truncated archives because the footer declares intended total length, but §4.4 puts that length in a trailer at file end, which truncation removes.
research_needed: Truncation experiments at many offsets across STREAM and INDEXED layouts; determine what a reader can recover without the trailer.
decision_needed: Where else (preamble, periodic sync records) is total length or entry map recoverable after truncation?

statement: Uncompressed tar degrades gracefully under damage, compressed tar does not, and ZIP typically loses everything if the central directory is lost (local headers may permit scan-based salvage).
research_needed: Damage experiments with incumbent salvage tools (e.g. zip -FF, tar --ignore-zeros).

statement: Entrybound is designed to answer which entries are damaged, not to survive damage; surviving damage is deliberately left to other tools (§22.5).
Digest algorithm selection is deferred to §25.
research_needed: Evaluate candidates for speed, tree capability, standardisation, FIPS status and long-term security.
decision_needed: Which single digest algorithm does format version 1 use?

statement: Exactly one digest algorithm per format version, with no negotiation.
A tree-capable hash function is preferred so that tree structure and hash agree rather than being layered.
research_needed: Reconcile with any later authority selecting a non-tree hash (e.g. SHA-256 in the crypto suite).

statement: The digest algorithm identifier must be bound into each of the LAI, PCR and AUX descriptors so future migration is unambiguous.
